entry.title: Universal opt-in replay protection?
entry.summary:
The proposal to introduce opt-in replay protection in the event of a fork war is based on the challenges stakeholders face during such conflicts, particularly when there is no inherent replay protection. This idea stems from recent difficulties experienced by those attempting to split their coins during chain splits, which has shown to be a complex process. The suggested method involves standardizing a 34-byte Annex payload that includes a specific prior block hash (`<0xFAF0><32-byte-prior-block-hash>`). This would function under normal transaction validation rules but would add an additional layer during block validation or template construction, requiring that the current valid header chain with the most work should contain this hash.
Furthermore, because Taproot signatures are designed to commit to the annex, they would inherently commit to a specific chain if a split occurs. This feature remains flexible as an empty Annex would still maintain validity across all potential chains post-fork. The system could also influence miner behavior, encouraging them to focus on particular blocks or facilitating actions like coin splitting for strategic dumps on targeted chains. Such mechanisms would provide tools for users and miners to navigate chain splits more safely and deliberately, potentially even if only one of the chains implements this rule.
Another point of concern discussed is the scenario where miners might attempt to introduce more inflation into Bitcoin through a hard fork. In such cases, if the majority of hash power shifts away from the legacy chain without replay protection, it would significantly impede UTXO holders' ability to express their economic preferences securely and effectively. This highlights the necessity for measures like the proposed replay protection to safeguard user interests during tumultuous periods of blockchain forks.
